name: Orrin I
about: Orrin I stands at the dividing line between Mediran history and Mediran legend. The Nine Oaths, his coronation at Brighthold, and the early works of his reign are well attested, but fourteen centuries of retelling have made the man himself harder to separate from the Unifier of popular memory. The earliest chronicles consistently describe a plain-spoken and imposing king who had little taste for unnecessary court ceremony and spent heavily instead on roads, granaries, market towns, and the first institutions meant to bind the Nine Realms together. Crown road crews included priests who maintained _Continual Flame_ at major waystones and mages capable of _Stone Shape_ for cuts where ordinary labor would have taken a season. His seventy-year reign gave the new kingdom time to become ordinary: children were born who had never known the realms as separate crowns, trade began to follow the new royal roads, and the Caelric household grew into a large and highly visible dynasty. Later traditions associate Orrin with the great shepherd dogs kept at the early Brighthold court and claim he continued to walk among stablehands, builders, and soldiers with considerably less ceremony than his household preferred, though such stories are difficult to verify at this distance. His epithet appears very early in the record and has never seriously been challenged; whatever later generations added to Orrin the man, **the Unifier** remains a literal description of what he accomplished.

name: Maerys
about: Maerys had married Orrin before there was a Unified Crown and retained habits formed before either of them lived as royalty. Early household accounts associate her particularly with provisioning, household wages, and the practical management of the rapidly expanding Caelric court, and later tradition credits her with resisting attempts to make Brighthold more lavish than the young Crown could afford. She also maintained close ties with families from the countryside around Bramblefold long after becoming queen. Popular stories frequently cast her as the person most willing to contradict Orrin openly; whether every exchange attributed to them is genuine, Mediran tradition consistently remembers the first royal marriage as a partnership rather than an ornament of Unification.

name: Princess Alessa
about: Princess Alessa kept the household rolls of early Brighthold once her mother's hands grew too stiff to write them, and several of her ledgers survive in the royal archive.

name: Prince Oswyn
about: Prince Oswyn spent most of his life with the Crown road crews his father founded and is buried beside the first waystone on the Westerhold road.

name: Princess Elyn
about: Princess Elyn bred the great shepherd dogs of the early court, and most of the royal kennel lines in Medir claim descent from her animals.

name: Maelor I
about: Maelor inherited the Crown at fifty-nine and held it for nearly ninety years, his half-elven blood carrying him well into a second century of life. The first royal libraries and the earliest college halls at Brighthold date chiefly to his reign, as do substantial collections of copied histories from the former Nine Realms. Restricted rooms were among the first royal archives regularly protected by _Arcane Lock_, while _Continual Flame_ lamps let copying houses work without smoke near old parchment. Music also became a regular feature of the royal court, with surviving accounts naming singers, instrumentalists, and several early practitioners of formal arcane study among those supported by the Crown. Later writers consistently portray Maelor as highly educated, eloquent, and somewhat severe toward those who were not; the old saying that he “heard the manner before the matter” appears in several versions centuries after his death. Whether he was truly as vain about good speech as tradition makes him is uncertain, but his reign firmly established literacy, scholarship, and cultivated expression as things a Caelric court was expected to patronize. **The Lettered** was originally praise and has remained so.

name: Lyrielle
about: Lyrielle was half-elven and developed a reputation for finding talented people before they were polished enough to impress her husband. Petitioners, provincial scholars, musicians, and minor household retainers appear with unusual frequency in records connected to her apartments, where access was considerably less formal than at Maelor’s public court. Several later royal patronage customs may have developed from these gatherings. A small body of court verse also depicts her as quick-witted and fond of puncturing scholarly pretension, though it is difficult to know how much the poets improved their patron after the fact.

name: Prince Adrian
about: Eldest son of Maelor I, Prince Adrian died of a fever at thirty-eight, eleven years before his father, leaving an unfinished history of the Nine Realms on his desk.

name: Prince Aemar
about: Prince Aemar drowned crossing the Amberflow in flood season while carrying copied manuscripts to the new college at the Stone Spires.

name: Princess Orrelle
about: Princess Orrelle married into House Verdayne and spent her long life supporting the court musicians her mother had first gathered.

name: Corwin I
about: Corwin inherited unexpectedly after his two elder brothers predeceased their father. His forty-five years are remembered for the **royal autumn hunt**, which began as a courtly gathering and developed into one of the principal instruments of his rule. Druids and royal rangers accompanied the hunts, using _Speak with Animals_ and _Locate Animals or Plants_ when needed to follow migrations, though Corwin reportedly forbade magic that guaranteed the kill. Each year Corwin invited lords whose disputes had occupied the Crown through the summer to ride together in Thornmarch and the Crownsward, where quarrels over boundaries, tolls, marriages, and old injuries were often settled away from the formal benches of the High Forum. The hunts were not peaceful in the gentle sense: competition was encouraged, rival houses were deliberately matched against one another, and the king appears to have believed that men who could pursue the same quarry without drawing steel upon each other could usually be brought to terms afterward. Surviving settlements from his reign often bind former rivals into reciprocal duties rather than simply finding one side right and the other wrong. No major war between the great houses broke out during his reign, and **the Autumn King** became inseparable from the season in which he did most of his governing.

name: Ryssa
about: Ryssa was an accomplished rider and hunter in her own right and appears to have played a deliberate role in the social arrangements surrounding the royal hunts. Guest lists and household records suggest that rival heirs were often lodged, seated, or assigned to hunting parties in combinations too convenient to be accidental. She rode her final recorded autumn hunt at about sixty and was remembered as intensely competitive even in friendly contests. Later songs give her impossible shots and tireless horses; the surviving hunting rolls establish enough without them.

name: Prince Alden
about: Eldest son of Corwin I, Prince Alden was thrown from his horse during the autumn hunt of 193 and died of his injuries before winter.

name: Princess Cerys
about: Princess Cerys rode in every autumn hunt of her father's reign and was said to have outshot her mother at least once, a claim Queen Ryssa denied to the end of her life.

name: Aemrys I
about: Few Caelrics received an epithet less flattering in life and more sympathetic in retrospect. Aemrys inherited at forty and spent much of the next forty-four years contending with drought in the south, raiding along the eastern waters, failed harvests, and the repeated expense of moving food and soldiers between threatened regions. Crown priests cast _Create Food and Water_ and druids used _Plant Growth_ where they could, but such magic could rescue a village or a field, not replace rain across a realm. Contemporary complaints portray him as dour, parsimonious, and perpetually expecting the next calamity; later histories note that calamity usually did arrive. Palace expenditure rolls show a marked reduction in the royal table during the worst drought years, from which probably grew the old claim that Aemrys ate the same ration issued to the Brighthold garrison. He had four daughters and one son and married the daughters into four separate realms, creating the first significant collateral Caelric blood outside the direct royal line. His reign was not prosperous and produced few monuments, but the Crown remained intact, the southern settlements survived, and later chroniclers have generally judged **the Unlucky** more kindly than the people who actually paid his taxes.

name: Adira
about: Adira came from a Solresti house accustomed to treating food and water reserves as matters of lordship rather than emergency. During the drought years she took a direct interest in royal storehouses and relief accounts, and several surviving orders concern inspections made by officers attached to her household. Later tradition credits her with exposing nobles who understated their grain reserves while requesting Crown relief, an activity that made her popular with neither dishonest lords nor dishonest stewards. Permanent emergency stores established during the reign were maintained long after the droughts themselves ended.

name: Princess Valera
about: The eldest of Aemrys I's four daughters, Princess Valera was married into Frostveil, and the northern collateral lines of the house trace back through her.

name: Princess Iseult
about: Princess Iseult was married into a Selmarin shipping house and wrote to her father about grain prices for the rest of his reign.

name: Princess Rhiannon
about: Princess Rhiannon was married into Ironholt, where she is remembered for making the forge-lords feed their workers before their own tables during the drought years.

name: Princess Vespera
about: The youngest of Aemrys I's daughters, Princess Vespera was married into Solrest and lived to eighty-five, long enough to see the Parchment Reckoning begin.

name: Lucan I
about: Lucan I was, by the measures available to his own generation, a highly capable king. He established the Crown’s gold, silver, and copper standard, fixing the three metals into the system of royal coinage still used across Medir, revised port charters, strengthened trade, and left a treasury in better condition than the one he inherited. The new standard relied upon Crown-issued weights, warded mint dies, and assay offices where _Detect Magic_ and _Identify_ helped expose magically altered coin. He was equally skilled at turning one form of advantage into another. Royal marriages bought ships; ships bought favorable trade; trade produced coin; coin secured levies and support in the Forum. The difficulty was that Lucan applied the same fluidity to promises that other men regarded as fixed. Over thirty-two years, children and grandchildren of House Caelric were promised in marriage repeatedly, sometimes to more than one house, in return for immediate political advantage. The full scale of the bargains became clear only after his death and helped produce the Parchment Reckoning. Accounts written before 281 describe a clever and persuasive sovereign; those written afterward increasingly call him a swindler. His epithet survived both reputations. **The Copper King** first referred to the standard he established—copper being the royal coin most ordinary Medirans handled—and later acquired a harsher edge, as his promises came to be remembered as cheaper than the bargains they purchased.

name: Vaelene
about: Vaelene was a formidable participant in the commercial life of the reign rather than simply its Selmarin connection. Port correspondence places her in negotiations concerning shipping rights, harbor dues, merchant disputes, and Crown financing, and several profitable reforms traditionally attributed to Lucan appear first in papers passing through her household. She seems to have shared her husband’s appetite for bargaining while possessing considerably less enthusiasm for promises that could not actually be kept. A few surviving letters warn against treating obligations as though they could always be exchanged for some newer advantage, although later chroniclers understandably made more of those warnings after the Parchment Reckoning.

name: Princess Merryn
about: Princess Merryn was promised in marriage to three different houses before her twentieth birthday, and one of those contracts was among the parchments burned in the Oathwood.

name: Daric I
about: Daric was twenty when crowned and inherited a crisis already older than much of his adult life. His answer to the Parchment Reckoning was very different from Aenor’s: where his brother had tried to determine which agreements were true, Daric tried to satisfy them. Marriage promises were honored where possible, and where they were not, houses received offices, estates, payments, or other concessions. Some settlements were made in spellwork as readily as coin: warded storehouses, _Continual Flame_ beacons, and Crown artificers appear beside estates and offices in the surviving grants. The surviving grants make the scale of the effort plain. Daric appears to have genuinely wanted a settlement in which no house could say the Crown had taken its price and given nothing in return, but royal recognition also gave doubtful parchments a legitimacy they might never have possessed otherwise. The treasury emptied rapidly, and the number of claimants did not. Later histories generally remember him as generous rather than foolish, though the two qualities proved expensive in combination. **The Open-Handed** was already in use before his death at twenty-three.

name: Sygrid
about: Sygrid entered court with the unusual burden of everyone knowing that her marriage contract had helped place her husband upon the throne. She responded by establishing a household notably independent of both Daric’s ministers and her Hallenskar kin, and took a direct role in receiving houses seeking settlement under the king’s policy. Several accounts describe her as blunt about the difference between what a claimant believed was owed and what the Crown could realistically provide.

name: Princess Alyra
about: Daric I's only child was an infant when he died; Princess Alyra was raised at Orrin II's court and later managed the ferry charities founded by Queen Wenna.

name: Princess Nerissa
about: Princess Nerissa testified before the High Forum about which of her father's bargains she had witnessed, and she refused to put her seal to any agreement for the rest of her life.

name: Aenor
about: Aenor inherited his father’s Crown and almost immediately became answerable for his father’s promises. His four-year reign survives largely in Forum proceedings, petitions, examinations of contracts, and records of the violence that followed attempts to prove or destroy them. The evidence suggests a conscientious ruler who continued to believe that the Parchment Reckoning could be settled if the Crown determined which agreements were genuine and then judged them fairly. That task became increasingly impossible as archives burned, seals were stolen, witnesses disappeared, and _Zone of Truth_ and other truth-binding magic proved unable to resolve what honest witnesses themselves did not know. Later portraits traditionally show Aenor thin-faced and prematurely aged, although none is securely contemporary. He died suddenly at thirty-six with no cause publicly established. **The Beleaguered** is less a judgment on his ability than an accurate description of a king who spent almost his entire reign surrounded by other men’s claims upon him.

name: Hedda
about: Hedda was a much harder political figure than Aenor and appears repeatedly in Varrengard correspondence pressing for firmer treatment of claimant houses and greater protection of their son Orrin. After Aenor’s death she became the chief guardian of Orrin’s interests while Daric occupied the throne and retained her own network among the houses that had supported her husband. Her later prominence during Orrin’s minority made her one of the best-documented early queens, though it also ensured that almost every account of her was written by someone with an opinion about House Varrengard.

name: Orrin II
about: Orrin was fifteen when crowned and sixteen when he brought the Parchment Reckoning to its symbolic end in the Oathwood. Rather than continue examining the disputed agreements, he ordered the Crown and claimant houses to surrender them together and burned the parchments upon the old oathstone. Several witnesses record that the fire gave no smoke; no acknowledged spell accounts for it. Orrin then married Wenna of Greyquay, a ferryman’s daughter with no great house or political bargain behind her, before the same gathering. The following year he issued the Ordinance of Nearest Blood, the **Counting**, removing the Forum’s old discretion over royal fitness. The remainder of his thirty-eight-year reign was much less dramatic. Orrin traveled constantly between the realms, and local chronicles preserve an unusual number of stories about the royal couple eating in modest halls, hearing village petitions, attending shrine festivals, and arriving where a king was not expected. Royal progress rolls regularly note _Sending_ between the traveling household and Brighthold, allowing Orrin to wander without making the court blind. So many places claim a personal anecdote about Orrin II that a fair number must be inventions. The affection behind them is not. **The True** came to mean both his rejection of false bargains and his reputation for dealing plainly with those he met.

name: Wenna
about: Wenna was half-elven, sixteen at her marriage, and the daughter of a ferryman from a small Jade Provinces trading village. She never acquired the polished distance expected of later royal consorts and appears to have resisted attempts to reorganize her household entirely around noble custom. Surviving stories repeatedly place her speaking directly with boatmen, traders, servants, and market women, and several river and ferry charities later claimed her as an early patron. Her low birth became part of Orrin’s settlement rather than an embarrassment to be hidden, and Wenna herself seems to have had little interest in pretending otherwise.

name: Princess Saeryn
about: Princess Saeryn spent her childhood on the road with her parents and could name the ferryman at nearly every river crossing in Medir.

name: Princess Danae
about: Princess Danae learned her mother's trade as a girl and ran the Greyquay ferry herself for one summer, to the horror of the royal household.

name: Maelor II
about: Maelor II inherited a kingdom whose most dangerous succession question had been settled but whose laws still consisted of royal ordinances, realm customs, Forum judgments, and surviving pre-Unification practice. He spent much of his sixty-four-year reign bringing those bodies of law into a coherent royal code. The code even fixed procedures for magical evidence: testimony under _Zone of Truth_ established sincerity rather than accuracy, while statements obtained through _Speak with Dead_ required corroboration like any other witness. He also presided personally over the final settlements of several feuds that had survived from the era of the separate realms. Legal writers of later centuries portray him as almost supernaturally patient, though surviving judgments do show an unusual willingness to let both sides exhaust themselves before the king pronounced a decision. Court inventories also contain a surprising number of carved games, puzzle-boxes, and pieces for games of strategy associated with his household, which later biographers have naturally taken as evidence that he enjoyed problems even when none were brought before him. **The Lawgiver** became standard within a generation of his death.

name: Cassia
about: Cassia concerned herself less with the wording of Maelor’s laws than with how royal authority was seen and understood. Coronations, Forum openings, investitures, mourning observances, oath ceremonies, and the reception of foreign envoys all became more formally ordered during her queenship, and several elements of modern Caelric ceremony can be traced to practices first standardized by her household. She was also a substantial patron of jewelers, metalworkers, and ceremonial mages. The later erasure of House Carmivelle produced the historical irony that customs Cassia helped establish survived long after her own family name was removed from many public records.

name: Princess Evanthe
about: Princess Evanthe shared her father's love of puzzle-boxes and built several of her own, one of which reportedly took the Violet Spires eleven years to open.

name: Prince Torrin
about: Younger son of Maelor II, Prince Torrin sat as a judge on his father's circuit courts and died at forty-four, two years before the king.

name: Rylan I
about: Few reigns acquired a more nostalgic reputation. Rylan ruled for eighty-five years during a period of unusually reliable harvests, population growth, expanding settlement, and relative peace. Census material suggests that Medir’s population nearly doubled during his reign, while new villages and cultivated land spread particularly through Amberfell and the Crownsward. Crown-sponsored druids used _Plant Growth_ around some new settlements and temple casters maintained _Purify Food and Drink_ at major granaries, useful advantages that supported abundance without creating it. The royal household was similarly large, with children, grandchildren, wards, and fosterlings appearing throughout court records. Rylan’s Carmivelle ancestry contributed to his extraordinary lifespan; he died at 141 and had been king longer than many of his councillors had been alive. Later writers tend to portray him as warm, domestic, and grandfatherly, a characterization probably helped by how many generations remembered having seen the same old king at marriages, harvest festivals, and court ceremonies. **The Long-Summer King** refers as much to the memory of his age as to any single season.

name: Elsbeth
about: Elsbeth, a half-elf of an old Fairweather branch, made fosterage one of the defining features of the Long-Summer court. Sons and daughters from houses across the Nine Realms were raised for periods alongside the royal children, and surviving correspondence shows the queen taking an unusually close interest in where young nobles were placed, which households suited them, and which rival heirs might benefit from knowing one another before inheriting their fathers’ quarrels. The system created friendships and marriage ties that lasted well beyond her lifetime. Her Fairweather upbringing also made her an active patron of harvest charities and rural household foundations, but it was the crowded, deliberately mixed royal nursery for which later generations remembered her most.

name: Princess Rhosyn
about: Princess Rhosyn ran Queen Elsbeth's crowded royal nursery in her later years and raised more fostered children than any Caelric before or since.

name: Princess Livia
about: Princess Livia married into a Greenreach family, and her letters home are among the fullest descriptions of Arborwyn to survive from her century.

name: Princess Yssara
about: Princess Yssara left Brighthold for Arborwyn with eleven of her closest friends, and near Mosswick they built a shared longhouse where everything from the cooking pots to the coin purse belonged to all of them and every decision was settled by the whole circle.

name: Prince Wystan
about: Prince Wystan is best remembered for killing the cyclops that had been smashing carriages on the Westerhold road, and the beast's skull hung over the Westerhold gate for a century afterward.

name: Corwin II
about: Corwin II appears in the surviving accounts of an extraordinary number of other people. Bards, enchanters, playwrights, architects, sculptors, artificers, scholars, and visiting mages all received money from him, and he founded bardic colleges in every realm while increasing royal support to the Violet Spires and emerging magical guilds. The king himself does not appear to have been a great artist or mage. His particular talent was enthusiasm for those who were. Palace inventories from the period include experimental instruments, enchanted curiosities, unfinished statues, unusual magical devices, and several objects whose intended purpose is no longer known. One contemporary satire calls Brighthold “a conservatory which has accidentally acquired a treasury,” a line later attached firmly to his reign. **The All-Patron** was affectionate when artists used it and less so when treasurers did.

name: Anariel
about: Anariel was a wood elf of Arborwyn’s ancient Sylvaris line and had her own strong preferences within the explosion of patronage. She favored works using living materials, older forms of natural magic, song traditions in danger of being lost, and artists willing to work outside Brighthold rather than gather permanently around the palace. Several royal gardens established under her patronage incorporated magically tended plants and living structures unusual elsewhere in the capital. Corwin was inclined to fund nearly anything that delighted him; Anariel was much more selective and acquired a reputation among artists for asking difficult questions before opening her purse.

name: Princess Elyra
about: Princess Elyra was a gifted enchanter in her own right, and two of her pieces were taken into the Violet Spires' collection while she was still living.

name: Prince Alveryn
about: Prince Alveryn rode out as a paladin in a company of heroes alongside a high elf wizard, a human cleric, and a dwarven barbarian, and Brighthold's bards lived off their exploits for a generation.

name: Aemrys II
about: Aemrys II remains the longest-reigning sovereign in Mediran history, holding the Crown for 146 years and dying at 170. His longevity allowed him to shape royal government in ways difficult for any shorter-lived king to imitate. Most importantly, the modern structure of the **High Forum** took shape gradually under him. Under Aemrys, urgent Forum summons by _Sending_ and magically warded record rooms became ordinary enough to appear in procedural manuals rather than marvel accounts. Earlier Forums had varied in size, privilege, and the relative strength of royal and noble voices; Aemrys spent decades adjusting representation, authority, procedures, and the division between the Crown and the Forum until the two-circle structure recognizable in the present day had largely emerged. The process was not one great act of foresight. Surviving revisions show repeated alteration when one side acquired too much leverage or when a previous settlement produced an unforeseen weakness. Later Mediran jurists sometimes write of the Aemrysan Forum almost as though the king had foreseen centuries of government in a single design; the records instead show a patient ruler improving the structure over the course of several human lifetimes. **The Forum Father** refers to the institution that became the defining work of his extraordinary reign: the modern High Forum, shaped and reshaped under his hand across nearly a century and a half.

name: Sable
about: Sable’s influence is clearest not in the formal structure of the Forum but in the practical politics beneath it. Her correspondence repeatedly asks who would actually accept a proposed settlement, which houses were likely to feel slighted, and whether a theoretically balanced arrangement could survive outside Brighthold. She maintained an extensive network of letters among noble households and was particularly effective at identifying objections before they became public confrontations. Aemrys refined offices and powers; Sable appears to have been unusually attentive to the people expected to live with them.

name: Prince Anselm
about: Prince Anselm kept the High Forum's procedural records for most of his long life and drafted the manual its clerks still follow.

name: Princess Corinne
about: Princess Corinne outlived her father, her brothers, and most of her nephews, and her last recorded words to the attendants at her bedside were "Don't trust _them_."

name: Prince Edwyn Caelric
about: Prince Edwyn was heir to the longest reign in Mediran history, married at eighty-five, and died at one hundred and eight with his father still on the throne.

name: Caela
about: Lady Caela was a half-elf of House Fairweather who married Prince Edwyn when he was eighty-five and she was seventy-four, and she died seven years before their son was crowned Lucan II.

name: Lucan II
about: Lucan II inherited after Aemrys outlived the intervening generation and almost immediately faced the **Grey Years**, a long sequence of failed harvests and regional shortages. His government imposed strict granary laws, restricted movement of food from afflicted regions, sealed some borders against uncontrolled migration, and punished large-scale hoarding with uncommon severity. Temple stores stretched supplies with _Create Food and Water_, druids used _Plant Growth_ where soil and season permitted, and _Purify Food and Drink_ saved spoiled stores, but none of those spells existed in numbers sufficient to feed nine realms. Palace accounts show the royal table reduced during the worst seasons, a fact later histories use to support the tradition that Lucan would not eat richer food than he permitted the city. He was not a popular king during the famine, and several provincial songs from the period are openly hostile to him. Later assessments are generally kinder: Medir emerged from the Grey Years diminished but without the wholesale collapse of major settlements seen in some earlier famines. **The Lean King** described both his realm and, according to later portraits, the man himself.

name: Sahrine
about: Sahrine had grown up in Solrest, where surviving a poor year depended upon preparation made during a good one. Her household became deeply involved in ration scales, reserve accounting, and the movement of grain between regions, and several measures traditionally called Lucan’s harshest appear first in memoranda associated with her officers. She was reputedly unsentimental about scarcity and intensely hostile to waste. Later Solresti histories often regard her, rather than Lucan, as the practical mind behind the Grey Years’ food policy.

name: Prince Edrys Caelric
about: Second son of Lucan II, Prince Edrys managed the provisioning of his brother Darian I's rebuilt fleet and died of a lung fever the year before the Regents' Contest began.

name: Iseult
about: Lady Iseult of House Verdayne was widowed the year before the Regents' Contest began and lived long enough to see her son take the throne as Lucan III, and to outlive him.

name: Lucan III
about: Lucan III understood that armies were not the only means by which a claim could be made real. Before taking the Crown, he spent heavily upon heralds, chroniclers, advocates, preachers, and hedge-minstrels who carried the same legal argument throughout the realms: no murder of Soryn had been proved, Daric therefore inherited lawfully, and the succession descending from him remained valid. In larger towns, enchanted placards and _Magic Mouth_ proclamations repeated the same phrases long after the heralds had gone. The argument was not invented, but Lucan’s skill lay in making it unavoidable. Contemporary allies and enemies alike describe him as charming, socially attentive, and unusually good at making a listener feel that agreement had been the listener’s idea. After the deaths at Wainsford removed the adult heirs of both branches, Lucan took Brighthold and ruled for five years through much the same mixture of persuasion, office, patronage, and coin. Opponents called those who repeated his arguments **the Chorus**. **Honeytongued** was used by admirers and enemies alike.

name: Ceridwen
about: Ceridwen was far less theatrical than Lucan and appears to have specialized in relationships that could not be maintained through public argument alone. Her correspondence reached wives, dowagers, household officers, temple figures, younger heirs, and lesser branches of noble families whose names rarely appear in the formal histories of the Chorus. Where Lucan won a room, Ceridwen was often the person still writing to its occupants six months later. Her surviving letters suggest a dry, observant temperament and considerably more skepticism toward her husband’s appetite for applause than his public court usually displayed.

name: Prince Aemar
about: Lucan III's elder son was twelve when he died with his parents in Emberfall of 736.

name: Princess Vespera
about: Princess Vespera was ten, and already twice betrothed by her father, when she died with her family in 736.

name: Daric II
about: Daric II is among the most difficult Caelrics to separate from his reputation. During the Regents’ Contest he rarely took the field, preferring letters, allies, private pressure, and the slow weakening of Lord Dace’s position. His enemies accused him of bribery, blackmail, hidden familiars, scrying, enchantment, and arranging the disappearances of men inconvenient to him. Some of these charges are plausible; remarkably few can be proved. After Soryn’s death the Counting placed Daric next, and he reigned for two years in much the same manner. Offices changed hands quietly, men vanished from court without public accusation, and the king himself appeared less often than most sovereigns of his period. Even surviving portraits are unusually inconsistent. His death from a “stillness of the heart” in 722 only strengthened the mythology around him. **The Unseen** refers both to the king’s private habits and to the sense that his hand was felt in events where it could never quite be found.

name: Ylva
about: Ylva responded to her husband’s withdrawal from public life by making herself unusually visible. She received delegations, attended major Radiant Path observances, heard household petitions, and presided over much of the ceremony through which ordinary nobles encountered the Crown. Contemporary accounts often describe Daric’s court through Ylva because she was the royal figure they actually saw. Whether this public accessibility counterbalanced Daric’s private government or was deliberately useful to it remains debated; either way, Ylva developed a political identity quite separate from her husband’s secrecy.

name: Rylan II
about: Household correspondence from Rylan’s youth describes an open-handed and sociable prince, noticeably different from the withdrawn king who succeeded Daric II. During his three years crowned, Rylan reversed attainders, released prisoners, restored confiscated lands, and reopened the investigation into Soryn I’s death. Sealed rooms were opened under _Dispel Magic_, old magical objects were passed through _Identify_, and diviners revisited surviving testimony, but no proof against his father was found. The king appeared less often at court as the inquiry continued and refused every marriage proposed by the great houses. In 725 AU he left Brighthold with a small party, a trunk, and a sealed letter declaring that he had found a wife in the Jade Provinces and was laying down the Crown. He named no successor. Provinces records confirm that he later married Nami of Isokaze and lived there rather than returning to Medir’s royal court. **The Eloper** began as mockery and eventually became an oddly affectionate name for the only Caelric sovereign simply to decide that kingship was no longer the life he wanted.

name: Nami
about: Nami was a Tabaxi pearl-diver of the Jaguar Clan and appears to have had little interest in exchanging her own life for the expectations of a distant royal court. Provinces records associate her with diving, coastal trade, and clan affairs both before and after her marriage, and nothing suggests she ceased those activities because Mediran heralds had begun calling her queen. She and Rylan built their life in the Jade Provinces on her ground rather than his. Much of what Medir knows about Rylan after abdication therefore survives because Nami’s community recorded him as her husband, not because Brighthold continued recording him as its former king.

name: Aldric I
about: Aldric was **crowned nine days after Rylan’s abdication**. The haste was characteristic. Aldric regarded uncertainty as dangerous and moved to secure Brighthold before distant lords could assemble or Princess Serica’s objections could harden into organized resistance. Once the War of Lions began, the same instinct appeared in his government through arrests, attainders, confiscations, and executions directed at suspected Couchant supporters. Rampant field commands kept dedicated war-mages for _Sending_, _Counterspell_, and battlefield wards, giving Aldric’s orders the same preference for speed that marked the rest of his rule. Rampant histories praise a king unwilling to let the realm drift into disorder; Couchant histories describe a man attempting to end every argument before the other side could speak. He died in 729 from wounds taken at the Stone Bridge of Wainsford. **The Hasty** therefore came to describe the instinct that set the character of his reign: to act before uncertainty could harden into opposition.

name: Vittoria
about: Vittoria understood better than Aldric that a defeated noble house did not cease to matter simply because the Crown had taken its lands. Her household maintained correspondence with wives, heirs, and collateral branches of several families under attainder, sometimes arranging lesser settlements or preserving property that Aldric’s harder ministers would otherwise have swept away entirely. This was not mercy for its own sake so much as dynastic prudence: Vittoria believed a king who left every enemy without a road back to obedience merely guaranteed another generation of enemies. She did not stop Aldric’s repression, but several houses later credited her with ensuring they survived it.

name: Crown Prince Severin
about: Crown Prince Severin renounced his claim under Serica's settlement, never accepted the renunciation, and died at seventeen leading the Rampant host at Wainsford.

name: Prince Selwyn
about: Prince Selwyn rode beside his brother at Wainsford and died there at sixteen, in the same fighting as the cousins he had grown up beside at Brighthold.

name: Wyllem
about: Wyllem was nineteen, baseborn, and possessed no uncontested place in the Counting when Lucan III died. He produced a document bearing Lucan’s seal that declared him legitimized, and the remaining Rampant houses accepted it because they had few alternatives. Most personal accounts of Wyllem come from soldiers rather than courtiers. They describe a skilled horseman, a gifted field commander, and a young king noticeably less polished than the trueborn Caelrics around whom the war had begun. Campaign rolls also show _Sending_ casters attached to his fastest columns, one of the few ways orders could keep pace with his cavalry. He appears to have made little effort to hide his birth or discourage the name **the Bastard**, which was used by supporters almost as readily as enemies. In eleven months he drove the remaining Couchant armies steadily backward and nearly ended the war at Redwatch. There, after finally cornering his opponents in the fens, the return of Prince Orrin and his winged companion reversed the campaign. Wyllem went from hunter to hunted with extraordinary speed, and his reign ended before its first anniversary.

name: Brya
about: Brya was a huntsman’s daughter from the country Wyllem knew best and had known him before any credible path to the Crown existed. Campaign records place her repeatedly with the moving royal household, where she took charge of remounts, camp provisioning, and communication with local guides who knew the Thornmarch country better than noble officers did. Later soldiers’ stories make her almost as formidable a rider as Wyllem and considerably less patient with ceremony. Whatever was embellished, Brya was plainly more at home on campaign than in Brighthold and never attempted to disguise the life she had led before becoming queen.

name: Princess Verena
about: Princess Verena kept her oath of renunciation for fifty-three years and was the only one of Aldric I's trueborn children to see the War of Lions end.

name: Darian I
about: Darian spent much of his fifteen-year reign rebuilding a royal fleet neglected during the Grey Years. Naval inspection records place him aboard ships with unusual frequency for a sovereign, and surviving letters to shipwrights show enough technical interest that later stories of the king working rigging beside ordinary sailors are not entirely implausible, though probably improved in the telling. He expanded dockyards, standardized portions of naval supply, and spent heavily restoring Medir’s ability to move force and goods along its coasts. Weather diviners sailed with major squadrons, _Continual Flame_ marked important harbor beacons, and rare naval mages able to cast _Control Water_ were treated almost as strategically as warships. In 716 AU, Darian was caught with a large part of the fleet in a storm off the Selmarin Gulf and drowned with roughly a third of it. The disaster left a nine-year-old heir and immediately preceded the Regents’ Contest. **The Sea-Taken** entered common use almost at once.

name: Corysande
about: Corysande was one of the last great figures of the old Maridane fleet house and shared Darian’s maritime interests more directly than most royal consorts. She had her own standing among Selmarin captains and merchant families and took control of both the royal household and her family’s fleet after Darian’s death. Her refusal to surrender Soryn to the High Forum was not passive maternal resistance but a deliberate claim that the mother of a child king possessed the right to govern for him. She died with the Maridane fleet during the Regents’ Contest, still defending that claim.

name: Soryn I
about: Soryn was nine when crowned and twelve when he died. The records of his reign are extensive but frustratingly poor at preserving the boy himself; nearly everything concerns the adults contesting his custody. Tutors’ accounts and household purchases offer the clearest glimpses, showing a child fond of falconry lessons, carved animals, and illustrated accounts of distant places. Whether these interests would have survived adolescence is unknowable. During his four years as king, his mother Corysande, Lord Dace of Brighthold, and his uncle Daric Caelric each claimed the right to govern in his name. Soryn was moved from the Silver Docks to Brighthold, married at eleven, and finally placed in Daric’s custody in 720. He died three months later from no cause that physicians, clerics using _Detect Poison and Disease_, mages, or diviners could establish. **The Boy King** is less an epithet than the fact by which history remembers him.

name: Greta
about: Greta was the same age as Soryn and had no meaningful control over the match that made her queen at eleven. She returned to Stonemarch after being widowed at thirteen and later remarried within Ironholt, where the greater part of her life was spent far from Brighthold. Granholm family records show that she eventually became a formidable household matriarch with strong opinions about marriages involving children and young heirs, and she repeatedly resisted attempts to use her descendants in arrangements concluded before they were old enough to consent meaningfully. Her thirteen months as Queen of Medir were therefore only a very small portion of a much longer life.

name: Queen Serica
about: Few Caelrics possess two epithets as politically revealing as Serica. To the Couchant houses she was **the Undoubted**, the daughter of Darian I and elder sister of Soryn I whose blood no opponent could deny. To the Rampant cause she was the **Lying Lion**, a usurper whose case depended upon accusing Daric II of a murder no court had proved. Serica herself never disputed the Counting; she argued that a man who murdered the person ahead of him could not inherit from the vacancy he created. After years gathering support from Wainsford, she defeated Aldric I in 729 and entered Brighthold as queen. Her scattered coalition had relied heavily on _Sending_ between distant houses, allowing Wainsford to coordinate supporters despite Aldric’s control of the capital. Her reign lasted only two years. The High Forum later ruled that Daric’s guilt remained unproved and recognized Aldric’s son Severin as having the stronger legal claim, forcing Serica back to Wainsford. She and most of the adult heirs of both branches died there in 731. The title **Undoubted** ultimately survived because her son Orrin III won the war and because even hostile historians found the word difficult to argue with on the narrow matter of her blood.

name: Gareth Merewyn
about: Gareth came from an old but comparatively modest Amberfellian house whose strength lay in Amberflow trade rather than armies or influence at Brighthold. He spent much of Serica’s years away from court managing the commercial and household network that allowed Wainsford to become a viable center of opposition, and surviving accounts depict him as more cautious than his wife about openly challenging the Crown before sufficient support existed. Once war came, he took command of much of the Merewyn levy and remained with the Couchant cause through its reversals. Gareth died defending the approaches to Wainsford in 731.

name: Crown Prince Soryn
about: Serica's eldest son died at eighteen defending the approaches to Wainsford alongside his father.

name: Prince Darian
about: Prince Darian was sixteen when he fell at Wainsford, where his elder brother and both of Aldric I's sons also died.

name: Orrin III
about: Orrin was a child when the War of Lions killed his mother, father, and elder brothers and drove him into safety in Solrest. He returned in 737 at fifteen, by then the last surviving son of Serica, accompanied by a great winged lion later identified as an androsphinx of the kind otherwise known from Orir. Its intervention at Redwatch broke Wyllem’s advance and transformed the political character of the war almost overnight. Whether Orrin rode the creature or fought beside it remains disputed even in early accounts. What is less often remembered is how practical his later reign became. After coming of age, Orrin enacted the Writ of Succession and spent forty-four years governing a realm exhausted by disputed inheritance. The androsphinx remained a celebrated presence at his side, but the king’s surviving judgments are generally careful, procedural, and far less dramatic than the art inspired by his youth. **The Winged Lion** ensured that the extraordinary return at fifteen would overshadow nearly everything else.

name: Soraya
about: Soraya belonged to the household that sheltered Orrin during his years in Solrest and knew him before he became either king or legend. As queen she maintained close ties with the Solresti houses that had protected the Couchant heir and became one of the Crown’s most important intermediaries there. She was also notably resistant to attempts to turn every detail of Orrin’s youth into sacred history; several court anecdotes preserve her correcting stories about the king’s exile or laughing at versions she knew to be false. Her presence helped preserve a private Orrin distinct from the Winged Lion of paintings and sermons.

name: Princess Nerissa
about: Princess Nerissa grew up beside her father's androsphinx and was the only person other than the king it allowed to touch its wings.

name: Prince Maerus
about: Prince Maerus died of a winter fever at thirteen, and the androsphinx lay outside his door for the nine days of his illness.

name: Soryn II
about: Soryn II inherited at thirty-four and spent ninety-one years repairing what twelve years of civil war had broken. His reign produced reversals of old attainders, rechartering of damaged holdfasts, revised trade agreements, new relationships between Crown and houses that had fought on opposing sides, and a High Forum in which descendants of Couchant, Rampant, and Chorus families eventually sat together without the old banners carrying immediate threat. Royal rebuilding contracts paired ordinary masons with casters using _Mending_, _Stone Shape_, and, on the most urgent works, _Fabricate_. He did not restore Medir by returning every institution to its prewar form; many charters and tariffs were rewritten entirely because the old arrangements no longer suited the kingdom that survived. His correspondence suggests a patient ruler with a dry sense of humor and little interest in royal self-dramatization. One later chronicler complained that Soryn governed exceptionally well and thereby left future historians “ninety years of paperwork and scarcely a proper disaster.” **The Second Sire** reflects the place later generations gave him beside Orrin I: the second father of the realm, rebuilding a kingdom that had survived the war but could not simply return to what it had been.

name: Marisol
about: Marisol came from a Selmarin merchant house whose influence was rising quickly when she married Soryn. She built a court around merchants, shipowners, guild officers, and port advocates who previously would have reached Brighthold chiefly through noble patrons, and became particularly interested in disputes where old feudal privileges collided with expanding commerce. Contemporary merchants sometimes found her difficult because she understood their arguments too well to be impressed by them. The Calvessar connection substantially strengthened the Crown’s relationship with Selmaris, but Marisol’s own reputation was that of a shrewd negotiator rather than merely a convenient merchant bride.

name: Princess Lysara
about: Princess Lysara had a vision that the Ascendants had promised her a parcel of land in Orir called Iz'Rii-Ell, sailed east to claim it, and never came home; word of her death reached Brighthold by merchant letter in 873.

name: Prince Evrard Caelric
about: Prince Evrard spent his working life in his father's rebuilding offices and is credited with redrafting more holdfast charters than any other Caelric.

name: Alyne
about: Lady Alyne of House Verdayne kept the household of Prince Evrard's rebuilding offices and raised the future Aldric II among its clerks and charters.

name: Aldric II
about: Aldric II is among the easiest early sovereigns to know because he devoted much of his life to ensuring that people like himself could be known. He commissioned histories of every realm, ordered copies made of older charters and judgments, sponsored surveys of monuments and tombs, and raised memorials to earlier sovereigns whether their reigns reflected well upon House Caelric or not. The most valued copies went into rooms protected by _Arcane Lock_ and _Glyph of Warding_, making preservation itself part of the Crown’s magical expenditure. His private notes and correspondence survive in unusual abundance and reveal the same preoccupation on a smaller scale: obsolete seals, genealogical puzzles, ancient coins, ruined foundations, and arguments over the correct wording of old inscriptions all interested him. Contemporary visitors occasionally complained that dinner at Brighthold could become an unsolicited lecture on a king dead five centuries. He was also the first Aldric in 145 years; surviving naming records make clear that reclaiming the name after Aldric I was deliberate. **The Chronicler** was inevitable.

name: Edda
about: Edda shared Aldric’s interest in preservation but approached it through stone rather than parchment. Granholm masons, quarrymen, and engineers worked extensively under her patronage, and she pushed for the repair of bridges, shrines, civic halls, and other ordinary structures alongside the grand monuments favored by the king. Several restoration projects survive bearing her mark rather than Aldric’s. Where he worried about whether future generations would know what had happened, Edda tended to ask whether anything built to commemorate it would still be standing.

name: Princess Orrelle
about: Princess Orrelle painted fruit for more than forty years, nearly always apples, and the royal collection still holds over three hundred of her apple studies.

name: Rylan III
about: Rylan III presents an odd problem for historians. His eighty-seven-year reign is well documented institutionally, yet remarkably little personal material survives for a king of his period. He governed through small councils, sealed large quantities of correspondence, and appeared less often at public court than Queen Eydis. Important packets carried magical seals or _Arcane Lock_, and some diplomatic dispatches traveled under _Nondetection_, making the privacy of his government partly literal. The kingdom itself remained orderly and prosperous enough that the absence attracted little comment at the time. The most controversial event of the reign came when the High Forum ordered the erasure of House Carmivelle; Rylan’s involvement beyond accepting and enforcing the judgment remains unclear in the surviving public record. Later generations naturally found the coincidence irresistible: an old royal house erased during the reign of a king famous for leaving little behind himself. **The Quiet** refers both to his manner and to the strangely muted historical record surrounding nearly ninety years of rule.

name: Eydis
about: Eydis, a dwarf of House Vyrskald, effectively became the public face of a monarchy whose king preferred private government. She received ambassadors, presided over major ceremonies, cultivated marriages between noble houses, and maintained the social calendar through which much of Brighthold’s politics actually moved. Contemporary descriptions emphasize an extremely controlled manner and an exacting memory for protocol; a lord might be forgiven an error once, but apparently not twice. Her visibility is one reason historians know considerably more about the social life of Rylan’s reign than about Rylan himself.

name: Tavian
about: Tavian liked systems that could be watched working. His reign rebuilt neglected royal roads, opened new routes between the realms, standardized portions of bridge and waystation maintenance, and substantially reorganized the Mediran Courier service after methods used in the Unaikei. Major waystations gained _Continual Flame_ markers, while _Sending_ was reserved for emergencies and _Animal Messenger_ supplemented ordinary couriers where roads failed. Royal itineraries show that Tavian personally traveled many of the roads while they were being constructed and repeatedly summoned couriers, engineers, and roadwardens to court rather than leaving such matters wholly to ministers. The changes shortened travel between several major cities and made written government considerably more reliable. Tavian and Kasumi had no children, a fact known early enough that the king used the Writ of Succession to name his younger brother Aemrys as heir rather than allow the question to gather into a factional dispute. **The Pathbuilder** therefore came to refer to both the literal roads of his reign and a general preference for making the way forward obvious.

name: Kasumi
about: Kasumi did not merely introduce Unaikei methods and then recede into court life. She maintained a small circle of Provinces couriers, navigators, and administrators whose practices were tested against Mediran conditions before adoption, and several of the final reforms differ noticeably from both the old Mediran system and the Unaikei model from which they began. Her correspondence suggests a precise, impatient mind with little reverence for inefficient custom. The couple’s inability to have children appears to have been treated by both as a private sorrow rather than a political failure, and Kasumi remained queen without pressure from Tavian to make room for another marriage.

name: Princess Talwyn
about: Princess Talwyn worked in Queen Camilla's plague houses when the Wasting reached Brighthold and died of it herself in 1070.

name: Aemrys III
about: Aemrys III shares an epithet with his long-lived ancestor for almost the opposite reason. The **Wasting** reached Medir in the early years of his reign and eventually killed much of his family, including several of his children and Queen Camilla. Ordinary disease still yielded to spells such as _Lesser Restoration_, but the Wasting did not; healing magic, alchemy, temple care, and mundane medicine could slow individual deaths without halting the broader plague. Camilla became known for visiting plague houses personally. After her death, Aemrys continued the same rounds, appearing in records of sickhouses and shrines across Brighthold for the remainder of his reign. Accounts from those years describe a visibly gaunt king who increasingly dispensed with large entourages and knew many long-term patients by name. The Wasting finally killed him at fifty-three, leaving a thirteen-year-old son. **Enduring** in his case meant continuing to appear where the disease was worst after nearly every personal reason to retreat behind palace wards had already been given to him.

name: Camilla
about: Camilla made the plague houses her own work before Aemrys ever inherited it from her. She organized teams of healers, temple servants, alchemists, laundresses, and gravediggers around several Brighthold sickhouses and repeatedly ignored requests from the royal household to limit her visits. Contemporary accounts make clear that she was not simply tending individual patients; she was trying to keep overwhelmed institutions functioning as deaths increased. Her own death from the Wasting transformed her into one of the most widely mourned consorts of the period and set the example Aemrys later followed.

name: Princess Cerys
about: Princess Cerys was eleven when the Wasting took her, a year after it had taken her mother and two youngest siblings.

name: Princess Corinne
about: Princess Corinne kept a bed of medicinal herbs for the sickhouses her mother had organized until the Wasting took her at nine.

name: Princess Evanthe
about: Princess Evanthe died of the Wasting at four, in the same year as her mother, Queen Camilla.

name: Prince Aemar
about: Prince Aemar was born in the worst year of the Wasting and died of it within his first months.

name: Maelor III
about: Maelor was thirteen when the Wasting killed his father and placed the Crown upon him. His minority was governed by the Regency Council, but even his early records show a strong interest in alchemy. Maelor eventually contributed to one of the first treatments that reliably slowed the Wasting, accomplishing through alchemy what _Lesser Restoration_ had repeatedly failed to do. The work survives in notebooks filled with revisions, ingredient substitutions, and the sort of stained pages expected from someone who actually used a laboratory rather than merely patronized one. His ninety-year reign became known as the **Replanting**: abandoned fields returned to cultivation, plague-emptied villages were resettled, trade revived, and the birth rate recovered over several generations. Maelor continued to maintain a working alchemical chamber at Brighthold long after the crisis passed, and later visitors remarked that the king could leave a formal council with clean cuffs and return to supper smelling of herbs and reagents. **The Sunrise King** refers to both his youth at accession and the sense of a kingdom emerging into morning after a generation of death.

name: Rosamund
about: Half-elven through one of House Fairweather’s old Arboran lines, Rosamund’s principal concern during the Replanting was not crops alone but households. The Wasting had left orphaned children, extinguished family branches, understaffed estates, and noble houses with more land than surviving kin. Her household coordinated fosterage, wardship, resettlement, and marriages intended to rebuild functioning families and estates rather than merely restore population totals. Fairweather granaries supported much of this work, but Rosamund’s surviving papers are as concerned with who would raise a child or inherit an abandoned holding as with how much grain reached the village. Her influence gave the Replanting much of its domestic character.

name: Prince Berwyn
about: Eldest son of Maelor III, Prince Berwyn worked in his father's laboratory from boyhood and died at thirty-five in an alchemical fire.

name: Princess Danae
about: Princess Danae oversaw the resettlement of plague-emptied villages across the Crownsward under Queen Rosamund's wardship scheme.

name: Princess Rhiannon
about: Princess Rhiannon was a celebrated court dancer and staged several of the famous pageants of her brother Theron's reign.

name: Theron
about: Theron inherited because his elder brother predeceased Maelor III and then spent forty-four years governing a kingdom with remarkably few major crises. He patronized playhouses, musicians, gardens, festivals, and court pageants, changed comparatively little in royal administration, and seems to have considered a peaceful inheritance something to enjoy rather than a problem demanding reform. Brighthold pageants of the period made liberal use of _Dancing Lights_, _Major Image_, and other illusion magic, enough that surviving stage directions sometimes read as much like spell notes as scripts. The surviving record is unusually rich in menus, performances, guest lists, and minor scandals. Theron appears to have been sociable, fond of spectacle, and genuinely liked by much of his court. Sterner historians later called the reign gilded, complacent, or hollow; surviving private letters from people who actually lived through it show remarkably little regret that their king gave them decades of peace and entertainment. **The Pleasant** began as a mild epithet and remained exactly that.

name: Elowen
about: Elowen was an accomplished singer before becoming queen and remained an active musician afterward rather than simply a patron of others. She commissioned new works, supported performers who fell outside the established bardic colleges, and was reputedly a much harsher judge of musical quality than Theron, who tended to enjoy anything performed with enthusiasm. Several surviving songs are attributed to Elowen herself, though authorship of the most famous is disputed. Court musicians seem to have loved performing for Theron and feared performing badly for his wife.

name: Princess Cerys
about: Princess Cerys studied singing under her mother, Queen Elowen, and was one of very few performers the queen ever praised in writing.

name: Prince Renard
about: A magical mishap during a court pageant turned Prince Renard bright green, and every surviving letter agrees he was insufferably bratty about it for the rest of his short life.

name: Corwin III
about: Corwin III brought a considerably more martial temperament to the Crown than his father, though his reign was principally about preventing wars rather than fighting them. He rebuilt the levies and watch systems of the border realms, restored neglected fortifications, and reorganized frontier obligations so neighboring houses and realms were expected to answer threats in recurring cycles of watch, warning, reinforcement, relief, and return. Major watchtowers gained permanent _Continual Flame_ beacons, key approaches were covered by _Alarm_ wards, and _Sending_ linked the most important frontier commands. Seasonal musters became more regular, shared patrols more common, and several old rival houses found themselves responsible for maintaining the same roads and warning beacons. Corwin also revived the autumn royal hunts associated with Corwin I, consciously invoking his namesake’s method of bringing competing lords into the same field. Later military historians credit his reforms with creating much of the border structure used during the following century. **The Warden** referred not to one victory but to a reign spent making sure a victory would be ready if required.

name: Maerwen
about: Maerwen was an avid falconer and frontier rider who accompanied more of Corwin’s border progresses than was customary for a queen of the period. She became particularly popular among Thornmarch officers after insisting upon riding sections of the watch roads rather than receiving reports from nearby keeps. Her household sponsored falconers, scouts, and messengers, and several improvements to the relay of warnings between isolated posts appear in correspondence bearing her seal. She was the third Dreymoor consort of the line and the last before the old house faded from major power.

name: Princess Alyra
about: Princess Alyra commanded one of her father's frontier watch companies in Thornmarch, a post no Caelric princess had held before her.

name: Hallard
about: The corsair wars of Hallard’s reign were more serious than his epithet’s almost adventurous sound suggests. Repeated attacks on southern shipping disrupted grain and trade, coastal settlements were abandoned or fortified, captives were carried away, and several important routes became dangerous enough to threaten the Crown’s hold on the southern waters. Hallard answered with twenty years of sustained naval war. Naval mages skilled in _Control Water_, _Gust of Wind_, and _Counterspell_ served beside marines and shipwrights, rare enough to matter in individual battles without making weather or sea obedient to the Crown. Taxes rose sharply, shipbuilding consumed enormous quantities of timber and coin, and the king acquired a reputation for refusing temporary truces that left the corsair fleets capable of rebuilding. Surviving portraits and veteran accounts describe a broad, heavily scarred man who preferred military company and had little affection for elaborate court dress. By the end of the wars the major corsair fleets had been broken and southern shipping recovered, though the taxation required to accomplish it remained bitterly remembered. **The Pirate’s Bane** was earned at considerable cost.

name: Nadira
about: Nadira’s work centered on the people Hallard’s war displaced. Her household administered temporary settlements, food allotments, ransom funds, and the difficult return of families to coastal towns after raids or evacuation. She frequently quarreled with military officers who wanted supplies reserved for fleets rather than civilians, and several surviving letters show little hesitation in reminding the king what his victories were meant to preserve. By the later war years, coastal relief had become organized enough that other realms copied parts of Nadira’s system during local disasters.

name: Princess Vespera
about: Princess Vespera sailed with her father's fleet as a girl and later ran the ransom office that brought home captives taken by the corsairs.

name: Darian II
about: The first Darian since the Sea-Taken king built his reputation without sharing his namesake’s love of ships. Contemporary jokes claim Darian II became ill on anything smaller than a royal barge; whether literally true, royal itineraries show a sovereign who overwhelmingly preferred to inspect ports from shore. He nevertheless understood maritime trade exceptionally well. Tariffs, warehouse law, port charters, merchant privileges, customs collection, and agreements between harbor authorities were revised repeatedly during his forty-three years as commerce shifted beneath older rules. Custom houses increasingly used _Detect Magic_ on suspect cargo and _Arcane Lock_ on bonded warehouses, folding routine spellwork into the machinery of trade. Darian rarely introduced a grand reform all at once. Instead, the records show constant adjustment as one route declined, another opened, a guild grew stronger, or a harbor required different terms. **The Harbormaster** began as a comparison used by merchants and became the usual epithet for a king who governed the realm’s trade as though he were forever watching ships enter and leave a crowded port.

name: Isaure
about: Isaure was famously numerate and had little patience for merchants who attempted to bury unfavorable facts inside impressive presentations. Several surviving anecdotes involve the queen finding discrepancies in cargo declarations or port accounts during meetings ostensibly led by Darian, and merchants appear to have prepared for her questions with particular care. She maintained her own correspondence with guild officers and harbor masters and was especially interested in corruption within customs collection. Contemporary observers often describe the royal couple as working partners, but rarely as interchangeable ones: Darian understood the movement of the whole system, while Isaure had a reputation for noticing exactly where its numbers did not add up.

name: Princess Saeryn
about: Princess Saeryn kept the customs ledgers at Orrinsport for her father and could reportedly spot a forged cargo seal from across the room.

name: Queen Rynelle
about: Rynelle was named heir by writ and became the first woman to take the Caelric Crown without a succession war. Her sixteen-year reign was devoted heavily to learning outside the great cities. Royal funds established schools and teaching houses in settlements too small to support them independently, while traveling instructors and copied texts carried basic letters, accounts, religious teaching, and practical scholarship farther into the realms. Many new teaching houses received smoke-free _Continual Flame_ lamps and warded chests for the books that were most difficult to replace. Her epithet arose from something more personal. Dozens of independent accounts describe Rynelle meeting a petitioner once and remembering the person’s name, family, trade, or earlier concern years later. One often repeated example has her recognizing a mason during a later progress and asking after a daughter whose fever he had mentioned at their first meeting. The sheer number of such stories, from unrelated sources, makes some unusual gift of memory difficult to dismiss. She died of winter fever at forty and was mourned across most of the kingdom. **The Remembered** thus acquired a double meaning: the queen remembered others, and they remembered her.

name: Bran of House Granholm
about: Bran concerned himself with the material side of Rynelle’s educational ambitions. School accounts repeatedly place his officers negotiating for buildings, arranging repairs, hiring local craftsmen, securing winter fuel, and making sure newly founded teaching houses had beds, ink, lamps, and roofs that did not leak. He appears to have disliked elaborate court ceremony and spent substantial portions of the reign traveling between projects. Rynelle decided where learning ought to reach; Bran became unusually good at making sure something was actually there when it arrived.

name: Princess Merryn
about: After an elven starreader cast her Ascendant trinity, Princess Merryn rode south into the swamps of Thornmarch and was never seen again; the High Forum declared her dead in 1400.

name: Aldric III
about: Aldric III was crowned at eighteen and developed an enduring fascination with what Medir did not know. He financed expeditions north beyond Ashenglen, south into Nothir, east toward Orir, and west into the Hollow and Silent Seas. His private rooms at Brighthold were described by visitors as crowded with maps, foreign objects, specimens, copied inscriptions, magical curiosities, and reports awaiting examination. Aldric was interested not only in geography but in secrets: ruined sites, unexplained magical phenomena, contradictory old histories, and regions omitted from otherwise reliable maps all attracted royal money. Many expeditions returned with valuable information. Others disappeared. Several western parties ceased answering _Sending_, while surviving reports from some journeys contain maps or observations that later scholars could not reconcile. Much of the stranger material was eventually restricted to the High Forum, Radiant Path, University League, or Violet Spires. **The Far-Seeking** therefore refers both to physical distance and to a king unusually unwilling to leave the unknown alone.

name: Sigrun
about: Sigrun shared Aldric’s appetite for discovery but not his willingness to believe every extraordinary report brought home by an explorer. She became known for demanding distinctions between what had been directly observed, what had been inferred, what divination had confirmed, and what a returning adventurer merely thought must have happened. Her household helped catalogue the royal collections and developed stricter standards for recording provenance after several embarrassing misidentifications. Aldric wanted to know what lay beyond the map; Sigrun wanted the map to say only what anyone could actually defend.

name: Princess Corinne
about: Princess Corinne sailed on two of her father's expeditions and catalogued their finds under her mother's strict rules of provenance.

name: Aemrys IV
about: Aemrys IV remains within living inherited memory, and there is little disagreement that **Mercurial** is a charitable description. He was intelligent, charismatic, curious, and capable of extraordinary bursts of attention. Early in the reign these qualities made his court exciting. New advisers were elevated rapidly, foreign practices were examined, magical innovations received royal support, rooms of the palace were repurposed for new projects, and policies considered immovable under Aldric III could change within a season. Surviving grants jump from _Fabricate_-assisted public works to elaborate illusion commissions and construct projects with exactly the same abrupt changes of enthusiasm. His marriage to Liriene, whose family had Oriri roots in the Jade Provinces, encouraged an already strong interest in ideas beyond the traditional Brighthold court. The difficulty was that Aemrys crossed into the next enthusiasm before the last had settled. Councils were reorganized and then reorganized again; favored ministers could fall suddenly; diplomatic priorities shifted; reforms were abandoned midway when some newer possibility caught the king’s attention. His moods were part of the problem, but contemporary accounts make clear that the whole government became mercurial around him. By his final decade, houses and councillors had learned to delay acting upon royal enthusiasm until they knew it would survive the month. His son Aldred inherited a realm weary of constant transition.

name: Liriene
about: Liriene shared Aemrys’s curiosity but possessed a much longer attention span. She maintained relationships with Provinces and Oriri scholars, merchants, and noble households after the king had moved on to some newer fascination, preventing several diplomatic and scholarly exchanges from collapsing when royal interest disappeared. Her own household became a stable point of contact for people uncertain whether yesterday’s royal enthusiasm still existed today. Contemporary accounts frequently credit her with preserving continuity without trying to stop Aemrys from being Aemrys, a distinction that probably explains why their marriage endured as well as it did.

name: Princess Valera
about: Aldred's younger sister, Princess Valera, died after a fall from her horse at twenty, two years before their father.

name: Aldred
about: Aldred inherited at twenty-six and has now ruled for thirty years. The defining act of his early government was the **Great Convergence**, three months of open councils intended to repair relationships damaged during the final decade of Aemrys IV. Where his father governed through enthusiasm and rapid change, Aldred developed a reputation for patience: he hears arguments at length, rarely commits himself publicly before he has decided upon a course, and prefers settlements that can survive the people who negotiated them. His reign was considered notably stable until the Vividness of 1448, after which Vivid Echoes, magical anomalies, and the political consequences of that event increasingly occupied the Crown. Royal expenditures increasingly record abjurers and diviners testing familiar tools such as _Detect Magic_ and _Dispel Magic_ against phenomena that often refused to behave like ordinary spellwork. Aldred is formidable in person but has little taste for theatrical anger, a quality often remarked upon by people who remember his father. His three children are now adults—Crown Prince Darian, Princess Lyanna, and Prince Corwin—and the differences between them are already matters of court interest. Unlike every ruler above him, Aldred has no settled historical epithet. He remains alive to complicate whatever name the chroniclers might prefer.

name: Isabelle
about: Isabelle came from one of the Ruby Cradle’s oldest surviving but never especially powerful houses, known for gardens, conservatories, flowering vines, and ornamental horticulture rather than armies or great wealth. She turned that inheritance into a political style of her own. Isabelle frequently received nobles in palace gardens and conservatories rather than formal council rooms and became particularly skilled at beginning conversations before either side was willing to admit that negotiation had begun. She maintained extensive private correspondence between households and was often able to keep disagreements from becoming matters that required Aldred’s formal judgment at all. Her death at forty-nine left the king noticeably more private, while Princess Lyanna inherited much of the diplomatic correspondence Isabelle had once managed.

name: Princess Lyanna
about: Princess Lyanna handles much of the diplomatic correspondence once managed by her late mother, Queen Isabelle.

name: Prince Corwin
about: Prince Corwin is a scholar of pre-Unification treaties who prefers the archives to ceremony.

name: Crown Prince Darian Caelric
about: Crown Prince Darian, heir to the throne, is a capable soldier who would rather drill with the Royal Guard than sit through his father's councils.
